processing: Coarse mature material is piled and pressed in the manner of Sichuan border teas; finished forms are fu brick and the bamboo-baled fangbao.
harvest_season: Made from mature, coarse growth rather than a prized spring picking, and coarser than the South Road material.
appearance_dry: Yellow-brown tea in a squared bamboo-strip bale with slightly tight corners, or pressed as a brick.
taste_profile: Mellow and clean with a slight smoky, scorched note.

brewing.notes: Simmer or steep long, as is usual for coarse border tea. Break compressed tea up first.

vintage_note: Sold as compressed or baled border tea rather than by fresh season. As with other Chinese dark teas it can be stored, so the production year and maker matter more than the picking date; old bales are rare and their claimed age deserves care.
description:
Xi Lu Bian Cha, West Road border tea, is the name for the frontier tea of the Guan county and Beichuan area of Sichuan. It is a family name rather than one product, and it is the coarser sibling of Ya'an's South Road border tea.

The finished tea comes in two recorded styles, fu brick and fangbao bale. The material is rough and mature, and the character comes from piling and pressing rather than from the leaf itself.

In the cup it is yellow-brown tea giving a reddish-yellow liquor, mellow and slightly smoky. Long simmering suits it, as with other border teas.

When buying, check which style you are getting, since West Road only tells you the family. Little of it reaches ordinary tea shops, so the fangbao entry is often the more useful name to search.
history:
The name separates Sichuan border tea by sales route: South Road and West Road. West Road tea came from Guan county and Beichuan in bamboo-strip packing, rectangular for Guan county and round for Beichuan. The round bale has since stopped, leaving the rectangular form as the standard.

An exact start date for the route is not well established.
